subjective.question: What is economics?
subjective.answer: Economics is the study of how society manages its scarce resources. It studies how people make decisions about what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce, because human wants are unlimited while the resources available to satisfy them are limited (scarce).

subjective.question: What is meant by opportunity cost? Explain with an example.
subjective.answer: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made. For example, if a student spends one hour studying economics instead of working at a part-time job paying Rs. 500 per hour, the opportunity cost of that hour of study is Rs. 500, the income forgone.

subjective.question: Differentiate between scarcity and shortage.
subjective.answer: Scarcity means that society has limited resources and therefore cannot produce all the goods and services people wish to have; it is a permanent and universal problem. Shortage is a temporary situation in which the quantity demanded of a good exceeds the quantity supplied at the prevailing price, usually because the price is held below the equilibrium level.

subjective.question: Differentiate between stock and flow concepts.
subjective.answer: A stock is a quantity measured at a particular point in time, for example wealth, capital or money supply on a given date. A flow is a quantity measured per unit of time, for example income per month, investment per year or saving per month. A stock changes only through flows.

subjective.question: State and explain the law of demand.
subjective.answer: The law of demand states that, other things equal (ceteris paribus), when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded of the good falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. This inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded is shown by the downward sloping demand curve.

subjective.question: State and explain the law of supply.
subjective.answer: The law of supply states that, other things equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied of the good also rises, and when the price falls, the quantity supplied falls. This direct relationship between price and quantity supplied is shown by the upward sloping supply curve.

subjective.question: What is the difference between a change in demand and a change in quantity demanded?
subjective.answer: A change in quantity demanded is a movement along the same demand curve caused by a change in the price of the good itself. A change in demand is a shift of the whole demand curve caused by a change in some other determinant of demand, such as income, tastes, prices of related goods or expectations.

subjective.question: What is the difference between 'supply' and 'quantity supplied'?
subjective.answer: Supply refers to the whole schedule (curve) showing the quantities of a good that sellers are willing and able to sell at every price. Quantity supplied refers to one specific amount that sellers are willing and able to sell at one particular price.

subjective.question: What is meant by ceteris paribus?
subjective.answer: Ceteris paribus is a Latin phrase meaning 'all other things equal' or 'holding other things constant'. Economists use it to isolate the effect of one variable on another, for example when stating the law of demand, all determinants of demand other than the good's own price are assumed to remain unchanged.

subjective.question: What are the factors which cause a shift in the market supply curve?
subjective.answer: The market supply curve shifts when there is a change in: (1) input prices, (2) technology, (3) expectations about future prices, (4) the number of sellers, and (5) prices of related goods in production. An improvement in technology or a fall in input prices shifts the supply curve to the right.

subjective.question: How can we identify whether demand for a good is elastic or inelastic?
subjective.answer: Demand is identified by the value of the price elasticity of demand, Ed = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price. If |Ed| > 1, demand is elastic; if |Ed| < 1, demand is inelastic; if |Ed| = 1, demand is unit elastic. It can also be judged by the total revenue test: if a price cut raises total revenue, demand is elastic.

subjective.question: Why is the concept of elasticity important in economics?
subjective.answer: Elasticity measures how strongly buyers and sellers respond to changing market conditions, so it tells us how a change in price will affect total revenue of firms, how the burden of a tax will be shared between buyers and sellers, and how demand will respond to changes in income or in the prices of related goods. It is therefore essential for business pricing decisions and for government policy.

subjective.question: What is the difference between an indifference curve and an isoquant?
subjective.answer: An indifference curve shows the different combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of satisfaction (utility); it shows the behavior of a consumer. An isoquant shows the different combinations of two inputs that a firm can employ to produce the same level of output; it shows the behavior of a firm in production.

subjective.question: What are economies of scale and diseconomies of scale?
subjective.answer: Economies of scale exist when the long run average cost of production falls as the scale of output increases, for example due to specialization, bulk buying and technical economies. Diseconomies of scale exist when long run average cost rises as output increases beyond a point, mainly because of management, coordination and communication problems in very large firms.

subjective.question: Why is the long run average cost (LRAC) curve U-shaped?
subjective.answer: The LRAC curve is U-shaped because of economies and diseconomies of scale. At low levels of output the firm enjoys economies of scale, so LRAC falls. After the minimum efficient scale, diseconomies of scale set in, so LRAC rises. Between the two, LRAC is roughly flat where returns to scale are constant.

subjective.question: Why does a firm charge different prices to different consumers? (Price discrimination)
subjective.answer: A firm with market power practices price discrimination to increase its profit by charging each consumer (or group) according to their willingness to pay. It is profitable because consumers with inelastic demand can be charged a higher price while price-sensitive consumers are charged less, so the firm converts part of consumer surplus into extra profit. It requires market power, separate markets and no resale between them.

subjective.question: What is meant by non-price competition? In which market structure is it found?
subjective.answer: Non-price competition means competition among firms on the basis of factors other than price, such as advertising, product differentiation, quality, packaging and after-sale service. It is a prominent feature of monopolistic competition (and oligopoly), where products are differentiated and firms avoid price wars.

subjective.question: Why does a monopoly have no supply curve?
subjective.answer: A supply curve shows a unique quantity supplied at each price. A monopolist, however, sets price and quantity together on the demand curve according to the MR = MC rule, so the same quantity can be sold at different prices depending on demand conditions. Hence there is no one-to-one relationship between price and quantity supplied, and a monopoly has no supply curve.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a firm and an industry.
subjective.answer: A firm is a single unit of production — an individual business organization that produces and sells goods or services. An industry is the group of all firms producing the same or a similar product, for example the textile industry consists of all firms producing cloth.

subjective.question: Why are marginal revenue and price equal under perfect competition?
subjective.answer: Under perfect competition a firm is a price taker: it can sell any quantity at the going market price and its sales do not affect the price. Therefore the extra revenue from selling one more unit (marginal revenue) is exactly the price of the good, so P = MR for a perfectly competitive firm.

subjective.question: Explain the circular flow of goods and income in a two-sector economy.
subjective.answer: In a two-sector economy, households supply factors of production (land, labor, capital, enterprise) to firms and receive factor incomes (rent, wages, interest, profit) in return. Firms use these factors to produce goods and services, which households buy with their income as consumer expenditure. Thus money flows in a circle: expenditure of households becomes income of firms, and expenditure of firms becomes income of households, while real goods, services and factors flow in the opposite direction.

subjective.question: What is meant by the market clearing level?
subjective.answer: The market clearing level is the price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied, so the market 'clears' with neither a surplus nor a shortage. It is another name for the equilibrium price determined by the intersection of the demand and supply curves.

subjective.question: What is meant by market failure?
subjective.answer: Market failure is a situation in which the free market, left on its own, fails to allocate resources efficiently. Its main causes are externalities, public goods, imperfect competition (monopoly power) and imperfect information.

subjective.question: What is a public good?
subjective.answer: A public good is a good that is non-rival and non-excludable: one person's consumption does not reduce its availability for others, and nobody can be prevented from using it. Examples are national defense and street lighting. Because of the free-rider problem, such goods are under-provided by private markets and are usually provided by the government.

subjective.question: What are subsidies?
subjective.answer: A subsidy is a payment made by the government to producers (or consumers) to encourage the production or consumption of a good. It lowers the cost of production, shifts the supply curve to the right, reduces the market price and increases the quantity traded.

subjective.question: What is Adam Smith's concept of the 'invisible hand'?
subjective.answer: Adam Smith argued that individuals pursuing their own self-interest in competitive markets are led, as if by an 'invisible hand', to promote the interest of society as a whole. Through the price mechanism, resources are guided to their most valued uses without any central direction.

subjective.question: What is meant by black marketing?
subjective.answer: Black marketing is the illegal sale of goods at prices above the officially controlled (ceiling) price, or the illegal trade of rationed goods. It usually arises when the government fixes a maximum price below the equilibrium level, creating a shortage that is exploited by sellers in the illegal 'black' market.

subjective.question: What is meant by minimum wage? What is its effect on employment?
subjective.answer: A minimum wage is the lowest wage rate that employers are legally allowed to pay their workers, fixed by the government. If it is set above the equilibrium wage, it creates a surplus of labor (unemployment), because the quantity of labor supplied exceeds the quantity demanded, although workers who remain employed receive higher incomes.

subjective.question: Define price elasticity of demand and give its formula. Also name its main types.
subjective.answer: Price elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded of a good to a change in its own price. Ed = Percentage change in quantity demanded / Percentage change in price. Its main types are: perfectly elastic (Ed = infinity), elastic (Ed > 1), unit elastic (Ed = 1), inelastic (Ed < 1) and perfectly inelastic (Ed = 0).

subjective.question: Explain the main determinants of price elasticity of demand.
subjective.answer: The main determinants are: (1) availability of close substitutes — more substitutes, more elastic; (2) nature of the good — necessities are inelastic, luxuries elastic; (3) proportion of income spent on the good — larger the share, more elastic; (4) time period — demand is more elastic in the long run; and (5) number of uses of the good — more uses, more elastic.

subjective.question: What is consumer surplus?
subjective.answer: Consumer surplus is the difference between the maximum amount a consumer is willing to pay for a good and the amount actually paid. It measures the extra satisfaction or benefit consumers receive from participating in the market, and is shown by the area below the demand curve and above the market price.

subjective.question: What is meant by the law of diminishing marginal returns?
subjective.answer: The law of diminishing marginal returns states that, in the short run, as more and more units of a variable input (e.g. labor) are added to a fixed amount of other inputs, the marginal product of the variable input will eventually decline. It operates only in the short run when at least one factor of production is fixed.
